hops.afterHeading: How you know a neuron is new
hops.title: London taxi drivers and a bigger hippocampus
hops.text: To earn an All London black-cab licence, trainees typically spend three to four years memorizing the Knowledge: about 25,000 streets and thousands of landmarks. Katherine Woollett and Eleanor Maguire scanned 79 trainees at the start and retested 59 of them about three years later, reporting the results in 2011. As a group, the 39 who qualified gained grey matter at the back of the hippocampus; the 20 who did not qualify showed no change. It is tempting to read this as adult neurogenesis. The scans cannot say. A bigger volume is not a birth record: more synapses, bushier dendrites or more glia could do it, though new neurons might contribute.

sources.citation: Woollett K, Maguire EA. Acquiring 'the Knowledge' of London's layout drives structural brain changes. Current Biology. 2011;21(24):2109-2114.
Transport for London. Knowledge of London Prospectus.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A black London taxi parked on cobblestones next to a tall stack of folded street maps and a brass compass.
image.caption: A bigger hippocampus on a brain scan is a clue, not a birth record for new neurons.

hops.afterHeading: Two places adult rodents keep making neurons
hops.title: Pregnant mice make temporary neurons for their pups
hops.text: Adult mice keep adding neurons to the olfactory bulb all their lives; in humans, carbon dating finds very little, if any, addition there after birth. Pregnancy shows one thing the mouse neurons are for. In 2023, Zayna Chaker, Fiona Doetsch and colleagues found that pregnancy wakes normally quiet pockets of stem cells in the mouse subventricular zone, with different pockets becoming active on different days of gestation. Their young cells reach the olfactory bulb in waves and become short-lived interneurons. Some of those subsets are needed, for a while, for a mother to recognize her own pups. The extra neurons are made for the occasion and do not last.

sources.citation: Chaker Z, Segalada C, Kretz JA, Acar IE, Delgado AC, Crotet V, Moor AE, Doetsch F. Pregnancy-responsive pools of adult neural stem cells for transient neurogenesis in mothers. Science. 2023;382(6673):958-963. PMID: 37995223.
Bergmann O, Liebl J, Bernard S, et al. The age of olfactory bulb neurons in humans. Neuron. 2012;74(4):634-639. PMID: 22632721.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A mother mouse in a paper nest sniffing three tiny newborn pups while faint golden wisps rise in the air.
image.caption: Pregnancy wakes quiet stem cells in mice to build short-lived olfactory bulb neurons for knowing their own pups.

hops.afterHeading: New neurons in the adult human brain
hops.title: Bomb carbon dates a Greenland shark
hops.text: Carbon-14 records when a neuron's DNA was made and can date eye-lens core proteins, which in humans form almost entirely around birth without replacement. In 2016, Julius Nielsen and colleagues reported lens-core carbon-14 measurements from 28 female Greenland sharks. The two smallest showed clear 1960s bomb-pulse enrichment, while a 2.2-meter shark had carbon-14 near the pulse's onset. The team inferred that the 25 larger sharks predated the pulse and paired marine radiocarbon calibration with a growth model anchored partly by that shark. That gave the largest, just over five meters, a 95.4% probability range of 272 to 512 years (midpoint 392), making Greenland sharks the longest-lived vertebrates known.

sources.citation: Spalding KL, Bhardwaj RD, Buchholz BA, Druid H, Frisén J. Retrospective birth dating of cells in humans. Cell. 2005;122(1):133-143. PMID: 16009139.

Lynnerup N, Kjeldsen H, Heegaard S, Jacobsen C, Heinemeier J. Radiocarbon dating of the human eye lens crystallines reveal proteins without carbon turnover throughout life. PLoS ONE. 2008;3(1):e1529. PMID: 18231610.
Nielsen J, Hedeholm RB, Heinemeier J, et al. Eye lens radiocarbon reveals centuries of longevity in the Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus). Science. 2016;353(6300):702-704. PMID: 27516602.

audio.title: Wild wheels, forgetful baby mice, and slow learners
audio.transcript:
Three stories about running, memory and new neurons: one from a sand dune, one from a nursery of baby mice, and one from a rat lab.

First, the running wheel. Adult lab mice given a running wheel have more dividing cells and more new neurons in the hippocampus than mice without one. For years, skeptics wondered whether lab mice run only because they are bored captives. So in the Netherlands, Johanna Meijer and Yuri Robbers put twenty-four-centimeter running wheels outdoors, one in a leafy urban green space and one in a sand dune, and watched them with night-vision cameras: the city wheel for more than three years, the dune wheel for about a year and a half. Wild mice climbed in and ran, in bouts about as long as those of six-month-old laboratory mice, and mice were by far the most common runners. When the researchers stopped putting food out for over a year, the running went on, and many of the runners were small mice, likely too young to have known the food. Mice were not the only customers. Shrews, rats, slugs and frogs used the wheels too, and some mice and frogs hopped off and climbed back on within minutes. The authors concluded that wheel running looks like a chosen behavior, not just a product of captivity.

Second, a twist about memory. It is natural to assume that more new neurons can only help. But wiring fresh neurons into an established hippocampal circuit is predicted to remodel the connections already there. In two thousand fourteen, Katherine Akers, Sheena Josselyn, Paul Frankland and colleagues in Toronto tested what that does. When they increased neurogenesis in adult mice after learning, the mice showed weaker memory on later tests, such as freezing less when returned to a chamber where they had received a shock. Infant mice make large numbers of new hippocampal neurons and lose early memories quickly, a bit like human infantile amnesia. Turning neurogenesis down in infant mice helped them keep their memories. And infant guinea pigs and degus, which make most of their granule neurons before birth, held on to the memories the researchers tested. When the researchers boosted their neurogenesis, both species did worse too.

Third, what it takes to keep a new neuron. Making one is only half the job; many die young. In nineteen ninety-nine, Elizabeth Gould, Tracey Shors and colleagues trained rats on learning tasks that need the hippocampus, and the number of surviving new neurons in the dentate gyrus doubled. The comparison tasks, which rats can learn without the hippocampus, made no detectable difference. Then, in two thousand eleven, Daniel Curlik and Shors looked closely at how each rat did on a conditioning task. As a group, rats that learned the response kept more of the labeled new cells than rats that failed to learn it. Among the successful rats in one experiment, those that needed more trials to learn tended to keep more of those labeled cells, though individual counts overlapped. When the researchers blocked N M D A receptors before training, the rats did not learn the response, and training no longer increased the number of surviving labeled cells. In Experiment two of that study, successfully learning the response went with better survival of the labeled cells, with a tendency among successful learners toward higher counts when learning took more trials.
